fields.meaning:
To do … completely
To do … decisively, resolutely
examples: My legs started to hurt, but I ran all the way to the end.
I can't possibly eat this much.
My husband came home looking utterly exhausted.
Everyone gave it their all, but we still lost the match.
I was deceived by someone I trusted completely.
The table was laden with more delicious food than we could ever eat.
fields.explain:
Expresses completing an action to the fullest extent, doing it completely.
Emphasizes a decisive decision or action, seeing it through without hesitation.
fields.notes:
1) ～きる (doing something to the end) is easily confused with ～終わる.
→ ～きる emphasizes “completely/to the fullest extent” and often carries the feeling of “using up everything”.
2) Not every verb can take it.
→ It usually goes with verbs whose action can be “finished off”: 読み切る, 使い切る など.
3) Be careful with the “decisive” meaning in your data (ghichu=2).
→ If you want a separate trap for the ghichu=2 meaning, the ct ghichu=2 entry needs an additional update.
meaning_vi: To do … completely, entirely…
explain: Attaches directly to the continuative form (Vます). Not used with nouns/adjectives.
Emphasizes perseverance/effort or a thorough result; carries the feeling that “nothing is left”.
In spoken language, ～切れない is often used politely to decline tactfully:申し訳ないですが、食べ切れません。
examples: 1. この小説は一晩で読み切った。
I read this whole novel in one night.
2. こんな量、私一人じゃ食べ切れないよ。
I can't eat this much by myself.
3. 彼は42kmを最後まで走り切った。
He ran the full 42 km all the way to the end.
4. 電池を使い切ってしまった。
I've used up the batteries.
5. 彼女は疲れ切って、その場に座り込んだ。
She was completely exhausted and sank down right where she was.
mistakes: Using it with a verb that does not fit the idea of “completion”: X 愛し切る (very rare/unnatural); use 愛し続ける instead.
Confusing ～切れる (ability) with ～切りれる (misspelling). Correct form: 切れる/切れない.
Confusing it with ～終える in a context that needs to emphasize “using up everything”: “在庫を終えた” → incorrect; it must be “在庫を売り切った/使い切った”.

examples: Ishida knew there was a test the next day, yet didn't tell me.
My mother is a terrible singer, yet once she gets hold of the mic she won't let go.
Young people these days have big bodies, yet they seem to lack stamina.
“You're just a kid (/You don't know anything), so don't talk like you know it all!”
＊Matsui doesn't do anything himself. And yet he complains about what other people do.
You knew, and yet you didn't tell me.
fields.explain:
Has a clearly reproachful tone; consider politeness in the workplace.
Often appears alongside words suggesting a contradiction: のに・くせに・わりに; くせに is the strongest in terms of criticism.
Suited to spoken language; in formal written language, replace it with 〜にもかかわらず (neutral) or 〜のに (softer).
Attaching it to stereotyped groups (〜のくせに about gender/age) can be offensive; avoid it.

～くせに: “Even though/And yet … (still) …” with a nuance of reproach, disparagement or sarcasm. It usually shows a contradiction between fact A and behavior/words B, together with the speaker's negative attitude.
• The subject of both clauses is usually the same person/thing (especially when reproaching the listener/a third party).
• Stronger nuance than 〜のに; avoid it with superiors or in formal writing.
• Can be used to reproach yourself: 分かっているくせに、また同じ失敗をした。
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～のに／～くせして.
→ ～くせに has a clear nuance of criticism/contempt and leans toward the colloquial.
2) Not used to state a neutral contrast.
→ For a neutral contrast, use ～のに／～一方で／～反面… depending on the sentence.
3) Often used when the speaker is unhappy with the other person's behavior.
→ A common trap, since the meaning is stronger than “even though”. explain: Used when you want to complain about or express irritation at something bad that happened when it should not have been that way.
The speaker feels displeased and annoyed about the matter ⏐ examples: 1. 知っているくせに、教えてくれない。
You know, and yet you won't tell me.
2. 元気なくせに、病気のふりをしている。
He's perfectly healthy, yet he's pretending to be sick. | Spoken variant: ～くせして
mistakes: Different subjects make it forced: “雨が降っているくせに、出かける” → unnatural. くせに fits when the same person/thing is being criticized.
Using it with superiors/strangers → rude. Choose 〜のに/〜にもかかわらず.
Confusing it with 〜わりに(は): くせに carries reproach; わりに(は) is a relative comparison.
JLPT: recognize the negative emotional nuance to choose くせに over のに/にもかかわらず.

examples: I was so embarrassed I felt like running away.
When I heard that news, I was so happy I could have jumped for joy.
It's about a 20-minute walk from here to the station.
If it's around 1,000 yen, I can buy it.
I'm so sleepy I can barely stay on my feet.
Is a size about this big all right?
fields.explain:
Position: くらい comes after the quantity/element being estimated, or after a clause expressing degree.
Emphasizing the minimum: “～くらいは/くらいなら” is used to expect a minimum level (“at least…”).
With a negative: “～くらいしか～ない” means “only about ~”.
Natural in conversation; in formal written language, consider ほど when talking about degree.

Approximation: indicates an approximate quantity/time (3時間くらい = about 3 hours).
Degree, intensity: states a threshold, “to the point that…” (泣きたいくらい嬉しい = so happy I want to cry).
Minimum/expected level: with せめて/少なくとも, expresses “at least…”.
Nuance: くらい has a standard nuance; ぐらい leans more toward spoken language (see the comparison section).
fields.notes:
“これくらい/それくらい/あれくらい/どれくらい” are very common phrases in questions and answers about degree/quantity.
In minimum comparisons: “これくらいはできるでしょ” stresses the lowest expected level.
“Vるくらいなら～” is a conditional pattern meaning “if it comes to having to V, I would rather ~” (a separate, advanced grammar point).
meaning_vi: About…; around… (estimate)
To the point of… (degree)
Only about…; nothing much (low evaluation)
explain: Expresses a rough estimate of quantity/time/distance… (not exact).
Expresses a strong degree: “to the point of…”. Comes after a clause/verb/adjective to emphasize degree.
Used to downplay: “only about…”. Often carries a nuance of low evaluation or treating something as insignificant.
examples: 1. ここから駅まで１０分ぐらいだ。
It's about 10 minutes from here to the station.
2. もう動けないくらい疲れた。
I'm so tired I can't move anymore.
3. ライバルに負けた。悔しくて泣きたいぐらいだ。
I lost to my rival. I'm so frustrated I could cry.
4. 彼くらいの背の高さなら、棚に手が届くだろう。
Someone about as tall as him could probably reach the shelf.
5. かぜくらいで仕事を休めない。
I can't take time off work for just a cold.
6. これぐらいの傷なら医者に行かなくてもいいだろう。
With a cut like this, you probably don't need to see a doctor.
7. 半年勉強したので、簡単な会話くらいならできる。
I've studied for half a year, so I can at least handle simple conversation.
8. 忙しくても、電話をするくらいの時間はあるはずだ。
Even if you're busy, you should have at least enough time to make a phone call.
9. 「こんなことを知らないのは君くらいだよ」
“You're probably the only one who doesn't know this.”
meaning_vi: 「～と同じ程度だ・～と同じ程度に…。」 程度の強さを表すために、ある状況に例えて言うときに使う。⑥のように、「～かと思うくらい・かと思うほど」の形でもよく使う。
To the same degree as ~ / just like ~.
Used when comparing something to a certain state in order to show degree.
The expression ～ かと思うくらい・～かと思うほど, as in example ⑥, is also often used.
examples: 1. この店のパンはおいしい。毎日食べたいくらいだ。
The bread at this shop is delicious. So good I want to eat it every day.
2. よう子さんの腕は折れそうなくらい細い。
Yoko's arms are so thin they look like they might break.
3. 天気予報によると、今日は台風ぐらいの風が吹くそうだ。
According to the weather forecast, there will be winds as strong as a typhoon today.
4. 傘をさすほどではないが、少し雨が降っている。
It's not enough to need an umbrella, but it's raining a little.
5. 突然立っていられないほどの痛みを背中に感じた。
Suddenly I felt a pain in my back so bad I couldn't stand.
6. さっき地震があった。本棚が倒れるかと思うほど激しく揺れた。
There was an earthquake a moment ago. It shook so hard I thought the bookshelf would fall over.
examples: 1. ①　３時間ぐらい
About 3 hours
2. ②　毎日、日本語を３時間ぐらい勉強しています。
I study Japanese for about 3 hours every day.
3. ②　〈駅で〉
A：すみません、黒(くろ)いかばんを電車(でんしゃ)に忘(わす)れてしまったんですけど。
B：どのくらいの大(おお)きさですか。

(At the station)
A: Excuse me, I left a black bag on the train.
B: About how big is it?
A: About the size of a magazine. (Showing with hands) Um, about this big.
meaning_vi: Expresses the degree of something by using an example
examples: 1. ①　死ぬほど
Like dying
2. ②　歯を抜いた時は、死ぬほど痛かったです。
When I had my tooth pulled, it hurt like death.
3. ③　夢に見るくらい彼のことが好きです。
I like him so much that I dream about him.
meaning_vi: 軽い程度・最低限を示す
Indicates a light degree / a minimum degree.
同じ程度の例を示す
Gives an example of the same degree.
examples: 1. 簡単な挨拶ぐらいなら日本語で言える。
If it's just simple greetings, I can say them in Japanese.
2. 今日は少しぐらいお酒を飲んでもいいね。
It's fine to have a little to drink today, isn't it?
3. 日曜日ぐらい休ませてくださいよ。
At least let me have Sundays off.
4. 卵ぐらいの大きさのパンを作った
I made a bread roll about the size of an egg.
5. うちの娘ぐらいの女の子が泣いていた。
A girl about my daughter's age was crying.
6. この車は私にも買えるくらいの値段だ。
This car is priced so that even I can afford it.
meaning_vi: To the extent of, to the point of, about
explain: Used to talk about degree or scale by comparing with things or events
examples: 1. それは米粒くらいの大きさです。
It's about the size of a grain of rice
2. この洗剤は、おもしろいほど汚れが落ちる。
This detergent removes dirt amazingly well
3. あきるほど食べた
I ate until I was sick of it
4. 宿題が多すぎて、泣きたいくらいだ。
There's so much homework I could cry
mistakes: Doubling approximation words: “3時ごろくらい” is incorrect; choose one: “3時ごろ” or “3時くらい”.
Using くらい for the negative comparison “Aくらい～ない” is unnatural; use “Aほど～ない”.
Confusing “only” with “about”: “三人だけ” (only 3 people) differs from “三人くらい” (about 3 people).
Forgetting the emphatic particle: to emphasize a minimum, you need “～くらいは”: これくらいは覚えよう。

fields.meaning: To tend to ~, to have a tendency to ~
examples: This job tends to get busy at the end of the month.
As people get older, they tend to wake up early.
fields.explain: ◎ Form meaning "usually becomes that way" or "is mostly like that".

examples: Next time, I absolutely want to pass.
This book is exactly what I've wanted all along.
“Nice to meet you.” “The pleasure is mine.”
This year, I really want to pass.
It's precisely in hard times that we should help each other.
It is only by actually using a language that you master it.
fields.explain:
Attaches directly after a noun/time word to emphasize the focus.
In ～から こそ, the second clause is usually a positive/desired result; the nuance is strongly affirmative.
Does not attach directly after verbs/adjectives (except fixed phrases such as から こそ); nominalize if needed.
Used in polite replies: こちら こそ ／いえいえ、こちら こそ …

• An emphatic particle meaning “precisely/exactly”: makes the preceding element the focus.
• Emphasizing a reason with ～からこそ: strongly affirms the cause-and-effect link (“precisely because… ”).
• Emphasizing a decisive point in time: 今日こそ／今度こそ express determination/high expectations.
• Used in reciprocal politeness: こちらこそ（a reply: I'm the one who should thank you/apologize）.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～だけ／～こそが.
→ ～こそ is used to emphasize “precisely… (is the one that…)”.
2) Often appears in fixed patterns.
→ Examples: こちらこそ, 今こそ, だからこそ… (emphasizing a reason/point in time).
3) Not a listing pattern.
→ Its main function is emphasis; it adds no new information. meaning_vi: Precisely, precisely because (reason) ⏐ explain: Used for emphasis when the subject is the main agent or main reason, to highlight it ⏐ examples: 1. 明日こそ勉強するぞ！
Tomorrow I'm definitely going to study!
2. 愛情があるからこそ、しかるんです。
It's precisely because I love you that I scold you.
mistakes: Using こそ directly after a verb/adjective: incorrect; use a fixed phrase (からこそ) or nominalize.
Confusing こそ with は: exams often test the emphatic focus nuance of こそ compared with は.
～からこそ usually goes with a positive result; choose the answer with the matching nuance.

rows: Weaker emphasis than こそ; こそ marks a strong focus
<ruby>君<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>はできる → <ruby>君<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>こそできる
Does not create a central focus like こそ

examples: From the way her voice was trembling, I could tell she was nervous.
Because a suicide note was found, Mr. A's death was ruled a suicide.
Was named … for the reason ～
That slope came to be called Fujimizaka because Mt. Fuji can be seen from it.

Triggered by ～ → change
fields.explain:
Usually followed by verbs of perception/judgment:分かる・見なされる・考えられる・推測される・判断される.
Use であることから in formal writing when it follows N/na-adj.
Avoid using it to state the reason for the speaker's own action (行く・買う・決める). In that case ので/から is more natural.
Suited to logical explanations in reports, science and news.

～ことから has two main uses:
• Basis for an inference/evaluation: “From the fact that … (we can) conclude/understand that …”. Emphasizes an objective basis.
• Reason for a name/origin: “Because …, it is called/was named …”.
• Formal nuance; common in reports, articles and news bulletins.
• Not used for a direct, volitional cause-and-effect relationship (buying, deciding…). When you need to give the reason for an action, use ので/から.
fields.notes:
• The naming pattern often goes with 呼ばれる／名付けられる／通称〜とされる.
• In essays it makes a good logical connector: データが示していることから、〜と結論づけられる.
• Position: very natural at the beginning of a sentence as a premise.
mistakes: Using it for a volitional action: “雨が降っていることから、傘を持っていく” → forced. Change to: 雨が降っているから／ので、傘を持っていく.
Dropping である after N/na in formal writing: “静かだことから” → incorrect; correct: 静かなことから／静かであることから.
Confusing it with からすると: ことから emphasizes a “factual clause”, からすると emphasizes “the source/basis N”.
JLPT: recognize that the following part is often 分かる・見なされる・呼ばれる in order to choose ことから.

rows: From the fact that…, hence conclude/name

Emphasizes the source/basis N rather than a “factual clause”
<ruby>症状<rt>しょうじょう</rt></ruby>からすると、<ruby>風邪<rt>かぜ</rt></ruby>だ。
Form that emphasizes the content of the clause
<ruby>不足<rt>ふそく</rt></ruby>しているということから、<ruby>増産<rt>ぞうさん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ。

examples: To my delight, I was chosen to represent us at the speech contest.
Unfortunately, Team A lost by one point.
To my disappointment, the camping trip I had been looking forward to was canceled because of rain.
Surprisingly, I hear the tickets for that concert sold out in 15 minutes.
To my delight, I got into my first-choice university.
Unfortunately, the meeting has been postponed.
fields.explain:
Usually comes at the beginning of a sentence/clause, followed by an objective fact.
Creates a formal, polite tone; suited to essays and presentations.
Not used for direct commands/volition. Used to express an emotion before describing the event.
With Aな you need “な”:残念なことに／幸いなことに.

～ことに: “How … that/It is … that” — puts the speaker's subjective emotion/evaluation at the beginning of the sentence as a formal/written exclamatory frame.
• Goes with adjectives/verbs expressing emotion/evaluation: うれしい・残念だ・残念ながら（different)・困る・驚く・ありがたい・幸いだ・面白い・不思議だ.
• Emphasizes the degree of the speaker's emotion toward the content that follows.
• More formal than て嬉しい/てよかった.
fields.notes:
• “驚いたことに/困ったことに/面白いことに/皮肉なことに” are common phrases in written language.
• It can also go in the middle of a sentence in a subordinate clause: 彼が来なかったのは、残念なことに、連絡が取れなかったからだ。
• With Vた + ことに: the verb should express an experienced emotion (驚く・困る), not an ordinary action verb.
mistakes: Dropping “な” with Aな: “残念ことに” → incorrect; correct: 残念なことに.
Using it with an adjective that carries no emotional nuance (例: 高いことに) → forced. Choose an adjective of evaluation/emotion.
Combining it with a command/volition: “うれしいことに、行きましょう” → unnatural. Separate the emotion and the suggestion using a different structure.
JLPT: recognize the sentence-initial position and the emotion adjective to choose 〜ことに over 〜てうれしい/〜とは.

fields.meaning: To make a point of doing…, habit
examples: For my health, I make a point of drinking milk every morning.
I hear that whenever Tanaka is going to be home late, he always sends an email.
When I was young, my dream was to compete in the Olympics, so I made it a rule to practice eight hours every day.
I make it a rule not to work at home on my days off, but this week I just couldn't finish by Friday, so I brought work home.
For my health, I make it a habit to walk 10,000 steps every day.
To save money, I make it a rule to eat out only once a week.
fields.explain:
Goes with adverbs of frequency/time:毎日/いつも/基本的に/～から.
Has a subjective nuance of a “self-imposed rule”; polite when needed: ～ことにしています.
Not used for natural phenomena/things beyond control: ×雨の日は降ることにしている。
Can be used to mean “pretend/treat as” in humorous or implied contexts:今日は休みってことにしている。

• Expresses a habit set by the speaker themselves and kept up regularly.
• Emphasizes a decision made earlier that is still ongoing. More stable nuance than ～ようにしている (which emphasizes “making an effort”).
• For rules of an organization/regulations, use ～ことになっている, not ～ことにしている.
• Most natural in the first person; other persons need context (a known/reported habit).
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ことになっている.
→ ～ことにしている is a habit or rule decided by the speaker themselves.
2) Confusing the nuance of “have already decided” with “am maintaining”.
→ This pattern emphasizes setting a rule for yourself and carrying it out as a habit.
3) Avoid using it for rules of an organization or circumstances.
→ External rules usually take ～ことになっている.
mistakes: Mixing it up with ～ことになっている: when asked about a “rule”, you must use ～ことになっている.
Mixing it up with ～ようにしている: if the emphasis is on “making an effort” rather than “it has become a habit”, choose ～ようにしている.
Using it for uncontrollable actions is unnatural (e.g., weather, automatic abilities).
Using it for another person without an introducing context → unnatural; add “彼は～としている/彼の習慣では～”.

rows: <ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby><ruby>更<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>かししないことにしている。
<ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby><ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>すことにした。

Emphasizes effort, may not be stable yet
